utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Harmon, before I invite you to continue the examination of the expert Brown, Judge Hanoteau would like to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: Good morning -- or rather, good afternoon, Mr. Prosecutor. I follow with great attention what was said yesterday. I said that it was very fast; things are going fast. Maybe sometimes a little bit too fast. What I wanted to ask you is the following: I was wondering if you thought of asking or raising a certain number of issues that would interest me, and I hope that you will not be surprised. I would like to tell you which issues I would like you to ask questions about -- rather, I would like you to ask certain clarifications from that witness. This expert report was given to us. I read it with a great deal of attention, and there are some points on which I would like to get some clarification from the witness, also to develop a bit more. A report, being a report, is a written document; it is a document that was pondered upon. And this is why I would like to get some further clarifications or some development. I would like him to develop on various topics. And with your permission, if you will allow me, I would like you to take down what I would like you to ask. In the report, there was a great deal of attention about the detention camp and of the way the roles between the police and the army -- the role was shared as to the control of these detention camps. The second point being the following: the second point that I am particularly interested in but the Chamber, as well, because we do discuss this when we meet outside of the courtroom: I would like to know what was the role of the paramilitary formations and those various groups, which role they played, and I would like to know a bit more on the exact position that the regular army had with respect to those paramilitary groups. In the report, we can read that some command officers were hesitant somewhat, and I would like to get more clarification on this. In that same chapter, I would like to understand if the army had to report to the civilian authorities, and if they were telling the civilian authorities what difficulties can these paramilitary groups cause. The third point is the following: In this report, we see how there was a division between ethnic groups. It is said in the report that the soldiers, the military, was -- or they were involved greatly in the division. There's also a certain mention of reactions of military authorities with respect to this policy of ethnic division, and I would like you to develop on this, as well. And I -- rest assured I have one last point, Mr. Prosecutor. In this report, we can see that there were some unrests in the army and that some people who were captured were killed. We can call them incidents, if you will. But I would like to know what the expert has to say on the reactions that the military authorities had with respect to that, to what happened. So I hope, Mr. Prosecutor, that those are the points that you will be able to elaborate on with the expert. I do not know what your strategy is; I also do not know what your agenda is and what you had planned to do today. I took the liberty - with the authorisation, of course, by the President of the Chamber - I took the liberty to call your attention on this, on those points which for me are real important issues. Thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau, thank you very much. It is my intention today to cover all of those topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one last point, and, in fact, before we resume, I would like to ask the witness to give me a clarification, with your permission, of course, Mr. President, and Mr. Prosecutor. That's all. Thank you very much. [Previous translation continues] ... before you brought the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, while the witness is coming into the courtroom, if Your Honours could take tab 6, which is the report on the army, I'll be referring to that immediately and very briefly. And we will be going to volume 2 of the documents. The first item -- the first item I'll be referring to is the small -- it should be in the small binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would already tell us the page, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Page 70 -- pages 70 and 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Brown. Mr. Brown, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Q: Good afternoon, Mr. Brown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Yes. No, Judge Hanoteau has one question. He indicated before. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a question for you. I would like to talk about the methodology used when you drafted your report. I'm just a little curious about one point. In your report, you talk about -- rather, there are a lot of footnotes in your report. Those footnotes correspond to what you call Krajina Corps reports or, also, 1st Krajina Corps regular combat reports, 1st Krajina Corps letters, VRS Main Staff reports. I'm just quoting you some examples. You talk about the Prijedor SJB reports. And I would like to understand -- I would like to ask you: Those reports were addressed to whom? Who they were forwarded to? They were drafted; we know that. But you do not tell us whom they were forwarded to or whom they were addressed to. I don't know if my question is relevant or not, but upon reading your report, I was wondering who was to receive all those reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously the report is quite lengthy and it does have many footnotes. Most -- or many of the 1st Krajina Corps reports that I refer to relate to reports that went to the VRS Main Staff. There are a number of 1st Krajina Corps reports that are disseminated down to subordinate units of the corps. The footnotes don't necessarily indicate which way. The regular combat reports went to the VRS Main Staff, or when they were the 5th Corps -- the JNA 5th Corps, they went to the 2nd Military District. So the regular combat reports went up. Some of the other 1st Krajina Corps reports are reports that are internal for the corps that were going down to subordinate units. So, for example, there's one document on the 10th of June which is a corps-wide instruction for further combat operations. That is disseminated down to the subordinate corps. There are other reports, some of the morale reports of the 1st Krajina Corps, were disseminated down to subordinate units of the corps. I believe that generally the Main Staff - I'd have to check the reports, probably individually - but the Main Staff references are ones that are coming to the Main Staff from the 1st Krajina Corps. The majority of these documents were formed or were found in part of the Krajina Corps archive, so they presumably were transmitted from the Main Staff down to the corps, and they kept a copy in their archive. As to the police reports, there are a number of police reports - - I would have to look, I think, again at some of these myself because I haven't looked necessarily at every single footnote more recently. Some of the police reports are internal; some, I believe, go from municipality to CSB Banja Luka. And I can think of at least one report that goes from CSB Banja Luka to the Ministry of the Interior. So I don't know if that answers your question in entirety. Maybe it was an omission of mine in the footnotes not to say exactly who the reports were going to, but it is a lengthy report as it is, and -- and maybe the footnotes would have become somewhat unmanageable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. No, in fact, you did not answer my question completely. What I would like to understand is the following: Was there a dissemination of these reports towards the state apparatus? There must have been a war ministry. There were civilian authorities that were dealing with matters, military matters. So these reports that were going to the Supreme Command or to the headquarters, those reports, were they also forwarded to the state itself? Were you able to find any traces of that? Or in other words, you talked about the Presidency yesterday; you've also talked about the Assembly. So I would like to know if in the documents that you were able to consult were you able to see, for instance, the military reports stemming from the head, from the lower instance? Were they sending that to, let's say, a higher-up hierarchy, and then, therefore, it was disseminated forward up to the state authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I discussed yesterday, I -- I think the combat analysis readiness report itself indicates that the civilian leadership or the Presidency, Supreme Command were made aware in great detail. It's a phrase that they used. There are -- I mentioned one of the documents yesterday about meetings that the corps commanders had to give to the Presidency. There's one on the 3rd of June. The -- there is the reference, of course, which I mentioned yesterday to the removal of non-Serbs from the army, a document which went to the Presidency, as well as to the Main Staff. There are references in the Presidency sessions of Main Staff officers briefing the Presidency at those sessions. So there -- and there was on the admission of the army a very good communications system, which included telephone links to the government. And I was shown yesterday the transcripts of some intercepts which seem to bear that there was a communication process. Now, we were hampered somewhat in the investigation in that we were not able to access or not given access to the VRS Main Staff archive, although that was requested many, many times to the various authorities, certainly during the time that I was there. And clearly the Main Staff archive, in essence, would find -- we may find the -- the material that's coming up from the corps and the dissemination of that material onwards. The 1st Krajina Corps was a formed corps in a chain. It -- it sat within a chain to the Main Staff. So it is not surprising to me that the main transmission method of the vast bulk of the documents from the 1st Krajina Corps is within that military chain. It is to its superior headquarters, which was General Mladic and the Main Staff. But even within that there clearly are some -- there is some evidence that they were able to send documents to the -- to the Presidency, and that one about the removal of Muslims is one. So there -- there are those transmission means I discussed yesterday. And also the transmission down, the -- the issue of the strategic objectives and their -- their appearing in military documentation, very clearly in documentation at the Main Staff level down, then transmitted down to the corps, and the corps then taking those references and using them as -- as their own means. It would indicate to me that there was clearly -- a functioning communication chain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. But can you tell us, with regards to these footnotes, if, for instance, when we talk about the 5th Corps regular combat report dated 25th April 1992, if we take that one, for example, could you tell us who it was sent to? Or is it extremely complicated to give us that information? You cannot, of course, remember or tell us from memory, but is it possible to find easily who was to receive all these reports that you've quoted here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that case, that specific example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, let's not take this specific example. We have many different footnotes here, and you mention many various reports. Is it easy for you to say who those reports were all being sent to, or is it incredibly complicated for you to find that out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the combat -- regular combat reports went to the subordinate military -- the superior military formations. Most of the Krajina Corps daily combat reports have annotated on them that they are being sent to the VRS Main Staff. In this example that you give, that was the JNA period before it became the VRS, and similarly there were same- structured documents that went to the JNA 2nd Military District headquarters in Sarajevo. Most of the regular combat reports do have an address of who they're being sent to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But may I insist on an answer. The question was how difficult it would be for you to verify who was the person addressed in this -- or in any other -- I mean, how difficult is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's not difficult because it's written in the document, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you would have to consult the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And are they available to you at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not -- not here. But I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If, for example, we would ask you to -- either give you a list or say for page -- this one to that one, please give us a list of the documents and then attached to it who were the addressees, would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would. Your Honour, I'd have to obviously receive some assistance from the -- from the Office of the Prosecutor because I don't work here now, but I would imagine that most of the footnotes have already been submitted, anyway, as part of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the support would consist of just having available to you the documents rather than any other support because as you may understand, an expert who further works on his expertise is supposed not to be guided by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. It's only to get accessibility to the documents, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: One point I might raise, Your Honour, is there is a DVD with hyperlinked -- or where the footnotes are all hyperlinked and you can just press "control", click, and just get the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All footnotes are hyperlinked. Do we have -- have we received that CD?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We can provide that, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm just thinking that it would be useful to the witness. I have a spare copy in the Defence room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's very nice of you, Ms. Loukas, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this includes English translations so that we can read, also, and understand the language?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps -- Judge Hanoteau, perhaps I can be of assistance to you, as well, in response to some of these questions because we will be getting to some of these documents. But, for example, if you -- just for your reference - we will be coming to it soon - the document that is found in tab 54, a very important document relating to paramilitaries, and that you'll see from the top of the document, the upper left-hand corner, that the originator of the document was the VRS Main Staff. And you can see at the end of the document where it was distributed, and you will see in this document, for example, it was sent to all of the corps formations in the VRS, the president of the SRBH Presidency to the SRBH Prime Minister to the SRBH army Main Staff commander. And if you'll look at other documents, you'll always be able to see either -- at the front page in the upper left-hand corner who the originator was, where the destination was, and if you look oftentimes on the rear page of the document, it will have the distribution list, so it will say exactly where it was distributed and all the formations. That's - - that could be of assistance to Your Honour. Now, Your Honours, I would like Your Honours -- we are talking about the 1st Krajina Corps, and if Your Honours could turn to tab 6, page 70 and 71. I merely point this out for the benefit of Your Honours. On the last paragraph in page 70, there is a paragraph that relates to the original size of the VRS, indicating that the total army strength was 177.341. And on the top of page 71, as of the 3rd of July, 1992, you will see a -- a chart -- not a chart, but you'll see a diagram that indicates the numerical strength of each of the corps, and you'll see the 1st Krajina Corps is strength at -- for combat strength, 43.128 men. And if you compare it against the other corps, you will see that it's the largest corps as of the 3rd of July, 1992. If you proceed to the figure 22 on the same page, then as of the time of this report you'll see that the strength of the army had swelled to 222.727, and the size of the 1st Krajina Corps was 72.330 persons. And you'll see once again that that -- size of that corps is by far the largest corps in the -- in the army of the Bosnian Serbs and not that figure 22 relates to combat formations. On the next page, there is also a chart dealing with non-combat units and services and the strengths of those, but I wanted to point that out to Your Honours so I could orient you and give you a better picture of the size of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, in relation to orienting Your Honours, of course, I think it would be preferable if the -- the witness were to provide that information, as opposed -- this is a marker -- as opposed to Mr. Harmon providing the information. I think it's -- we have an expert here, and I think the expert should be supplying -- it can be done very simply through questions and answers of the expert as opposed to Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it make any difference if Mr. Harmon would ask the witness to say, "What was the strength of the corps on the basis of figure 21," or ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I indicated, it's a marker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, the information has emerged from the mouth of Mr. Harmon in this circumstance, but I want to ensure that the questioning and the information comes through the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I take that as a general rule, Ms. Loukas. But at the same time, if we're looking at tables and charts, then it's just -- I would not -- well, it's a marker. Let's keep it to that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's a marker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, it's marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've noted the marker, Your Honour. I want to also note that given the limited amount of time that I have, I could ask four or five or six questions about a piece of evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- in evidence, and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the witness is here. If -- when Mr. Harmon draws our attention to something and if he would in any way give not the accurate impression of what you would read in this report, then please alert us immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to be discussing the strategic objectives, Your Honours, and this topic is found in Mr. Brown's report at page 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask one question in relation to figure 21 we just had in front of us. Independent units, 19.384, as we find in figure 21. What are independent units, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly what -- what they're referring to, but I do know that there were some -- they called them independent units at the corps level, which were not necessarily attached to brigades. They -- they sat as an independent unit that could be moved around very quickly within a brigade. So in our military, we would often call them some specialist units or -- they weren't attached to a division or a brigade. And that's -- basically it's -- it's another type of unit that was more flexible for the corps commander to use. But I -- I would have to look at it again to see exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would not be units from -- well, let's say paramilitary origin which more or less orbited around the regular units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of some documentation that paramilitaries at times, when they were integrated into the VRS, were integrated and called "independent" or, "assault" or "sabotage units." But often they were formed into a brigade, as part of a brigade, so they would be a small component of a brigade, rather than a large independent -- a larger independent unit. So I couldn't say from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's clear. Thank you very much. Mr. Harmon, please proceed. Examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, as I said, we're going to be discussing the issue of strategic objectives, and if we could turn first to tab 43 in Volume 2. These are the strategic objectives. Can you, Mr. Brown -- actually, before I ask that question, Mr. Brown, I'm going to try to get through a large volume of documents in a very short period of time, and to do so, we will go through some of these documents at a very quick pace. Could you look at the strategic objectives, and could you identify for the Judges which specific strategic objectives or parts thereof related to the area of responsibility of the 1 Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strategic objective number 1, number 2, and part of number 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part of number 4?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Establish a border on the Una River." That objective actually was split between the 1st Krajina Corps and the 2nd Krajina Corps, so it wasn't exclusively a 1 KK objective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Brown, turn to the next tab, tab 44. And, Mr. Brown, this exhibit is a transcript of the 16th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly that was held on the 12th of May, 1992, in Banja Luka. Why did you look at this document in preparing your report, and what is the significance of it to you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I began reviewing some of the military documentation from the 1st Krajina Corps, I noted that there were some references in there to goals or objectives, and I wanted to explore what that may have meant to the 1st Krajina Corps. And when I reviewed this Assembly session and especially the announcement of the strategic goals by Dr. Karadzic, I wanted to explore whether those political goals that were announced at that session were in any way tied or linked to the documentation that I'd seen in the 1st Krajina Corps and also the activities of the 1st Krajina Corps in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find references in this session of the Assembly that did relate to military -- conduct of military operations in the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps and elsewhere in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would argue that the six strategic goals outlined by Dr. Karadzic can be tied to very many military operations and not exclusively to the 1st Krajina Corps, which I probably know better than others, but you can link it to many of the operations. And as we discussed yesterday, there are a number of military directives that directly relate to those goals, and, importantly, there are clear examples of military operations that -- that are very much linked to the -- to the goals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a hierarchy in the strategic objectives that were promulgated on the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there -- I believe Dr. Karadzic himself said there was a hierarchy, and then I believe later on in the session Mr. Krajisnik himself said that ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to refer to a part of the transcript. Could you refer to it by page number first, identify the page number, and then make the reference.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, they're -- they're given numeric hierarchy on page 13, when Karadzic announces them. Mr. Krajisnik on page 49 of the translation said that "I would just like to offer an explanation since I also -- I have also taken part in adopting these goals. We must make a choice regarding one thing: The first goal is the most important one, and in relation to all other goals, all other goals are subitems of the first one." I think there was also a reference that Karadzic said that the Sarajevo goal could be switched, so he did talk about hierarchy of goals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 1.43 of your report, you assert that strategic objective number 1 would entail the movement of a significant part of the non-Serb population out of the new Serb state. How did you arrive at that conclusion, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there are a number of references directly in the 16th Assembly Session that would indicate that in achieving those goals, and in particular the first goal, that it would involve resettlement or the movement of people. There are a number of speakers there who -- who make reference to that. Ratko Mladic, I believe, is maybe the only speaker in the Assembly session then who -- who utters some words of caution and makes mention of people being moved. I can quote those references.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you do so, please, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, directing the Court's attention to the page numbers of the reference.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic himself says that, when talking about the first strategic goal, that "It's separation from the other two national communities, separation of states." But he goes on to say that "Separation from those who are enemies" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if I may interrupt you. You were invited by Mr. Harmon to draw our attention to the page number so that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. Page 13 on the translation, about halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Separation from those who are our enemies and who would have used every opportunity, especially" -- sorry -- "and who have used every opportunity, especially this century, to attack us and who would continue with such practices if we were to stay together in the same state." On page 16 of the translation, Dr. Karadzic also says, "We do not want to get in our state with a huge number of people who are against that state." On page 24 and 25, there is a speech by Miroslav Vjestica, who was an SDS leader in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, could you wait just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And Mr. Vjestica gave a detailed account of what had happened in Bosanska Krupa, including making reference to the fact that a large number of Muslims had moved out. And he himself said at the bottom of the page, "What are our adversaries doing? At the moment, they're all in the Kazin Krajina. On the right bank of the Una River, there are no more Muslims in the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa. All the enclaves that were there - Rapusa, Veliki, Verbovik [phoen], Ostruznica, Babic, Muslim Jasenica, and Zavir - we have evacuated them, so there will be none there for the duration of war operations. Will they have a place to return to? I think it's unlikely after our president told us the happy news at the right bank of the" -- "the right bank" - I am assuming it is of the river - "is the border." There is also a reference on page 17 -- I'm sorry, on page 18 - - no, I'm sorry, 19, which is a comment by Trifko Radic, who makes mention about the borders and separation, and he says halfway down the page, "As for continuing the war, please deal with this now. Please make sure that the lines of demarcation and goals are determined, and the rest will easily follow. I read reports on when the Swedes and Norwegians separated; the process of resettlement lasted ten years. We will see the same thing here, but it is still better to do that and know exactly who is resettling where. It will be a difficult process; it will require a lot of toil and effort and explaining to people who have to leave their hearths." There are two comments from Ratko Mladic, who himself, I believe, understands what -- what this implies. He, as I say, seems to be one of the few, if not the only in this -- surprisingly in this speech who -- who utters some word of caution. He -- he, first of all, actually says that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What page, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 33 -- oh, I'm sorry. Before I come to Ratko Mladic, there's a section by Professor Milojevic on page 33, at the very bottom. He's talking about maps and state borders. "If it is a state border intrinsically implies moving a contingent of population." Ratko Mladic on page 37 states that -- and he's discussing more widely that -- the objectives. He says, "People and peoples are not pawns, nor are they keys in one's pocket. They can be shifted from here to there. It's something easily said but difficult to achieve." And then later on page 39, he states --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you direct us before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, but where is it on page 37? This is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On a long page like this, if you could, Mr. Brown, please approximately locate on the page where the quotation you're referring to is located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. On page 37, it's at the very, very top, the first two lines. On page 39, about -- about 15 lines down approximately, Mladic says, "Therefore, we cannot cleanse, nor can we have a sieve to sift so that only Serbs would stay or that Serbs would fall through and the rest leave. Well, that is -- that will not -- I do not know how Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic would explain this to the world. People, that would be genocide. We have to call upon any man who has his brow -- who has browed his forehead to the ground to embrace these areas and territories of the state we plan to make." And so those are some of the -- those are some of the comments at the Assembly session that leads me to believe that there was an awareness that -- that resettlement was going to be a feature, and possibly more -- more importantly, when I looked at the documentation -- the military documentation from the 1st Krajina Corps, they themselves were not only aware that resettlement and the movement out of the population was occurring in the months after this Assembly session, but they were involved in that process, and some documentation indicates that they were clearly supportive of that process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, besides General Mladic and beside the representatives who -- from the various municipalities who were present at -- attending this session, were there other military personnel and other nonmilitary personnel that you're aware of who attended this particular session?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that Bogdan Subotic, the Minister of Defence, attended. I believe that General Talic attended. Milorad Sajic [phoen], who was a Territorial Defence officer and was the Regional Minister of Defence at the ARK attended, and I also believe that members of the Autonomous Region of -- or the Serbian areas in Croatia, the Krajina in Croatia, attended the meeting, as well. So it wasn't exclusively SDS; there were some military personnel there and members from the Serb areas in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, was the public pronouncement of these strategic objectives an epiphany to the people who were attending that session?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an inappropriate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I have the basis for that being an inappropriate question?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, firstly, it's -- was it an epiphany? It's leading. Secondly, the nature of the question. The use of the term "epiphany," I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's, before we --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The question has been objected on the basis of there's rather too much journalism in the question previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It seems to me there is a little in that, Your Honour; that's inappropriate. Number one, it's leading. There is -- it's an inappropriate legal question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's a legal question or not, whether it's an epiphany or not, but could you tell us how the public received the public pronouncement by those who were attending that session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not so sure I can answer how the public perceived the announcements, Your Honour. If -- if Mr. Harmon's question was about whether -- whether it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think -- I didn't ask how the public perceived it. No, I did so. I made a mistake. How was the public announcement received by those who attended the session? The public announcement of the strategic goals, I think it was. Yes, objectives.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it may be difficult in some areas for me to answer the question for those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please ask it -- if to the extent you can respond to the question -- answer the question, please do so, and if there is specific issues you'd say, "I couldn't say anything about," please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Reading this Assembly session, I don't see any, apart from possibly General Mladic, who issued some -- those -- those phrases of caution. I see nothing in there that would indicate that people disagreed with this, stood up against it, voiced opinions that they thought it was going to lead to problems, or that they whole-heartedly disagreed with it, reading this Assembly session. In fact, some of the language used by some of the speakers - in particular, Mr. Vjestica - would seem to be very supportive of it. I don't see any -- any debate or critical comments from this Assembly session. That's as far as I could tell you about the political leadership from reading this Assembly session. What I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any indication that this public announcement may have come either as a surprise or as something, well, that the -- those attending were well acquainted with it? Is it something of the kind you can observe from the session minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would argue that some components of these goals were already -- were already implemented, and I would imagine they could only have been implemented if they'd been aware. Mr. Karadzic, for example, mentioned that they already had Sarajevo in encirclement and that they had municipalities under their control. And -- and that would seem to be one of the -- one of the features that they would require to achieve the strategic goal in relation to Sarajevo. There already had been, I know in the Krajina in some areas, takeovers of power, and there had already been some military attacks. Mr. Vjestica had mentioned that -- what had gone on in Bosanska Krupa. Mr. Vjestica already in his speech was talking about the neighbouring municipality of Bosanski Novi and what was going on there. So even reading this and placing it with some of the documentation, I would find it hard to believe that it was a complete revelation at that time, and I don't believe that the 16th Assembly Session and the goals that were announced there were, in essence, a start point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, you said that there had already been some actions taken to implement these particular goals, and you cited some references. Can you tell us, to the best of your knowledge, where, in what locations, there had been efforts taken by the JNA or there -- by Territorial Defence units, Serb Territorial Defence units, or SDS party-associated units that started the implementation of these strategic objectives prior to the 12th of May, 1992? Can you identify some of those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanska Krupa was one municipality clearly highlighted there, and I know that elements of Talic's corps had been involved in that takeover. I'm aware of -- and that -- that was combat action; that wasn't simply just a takeover. I'm aware that prior to the Assembly session, only days before in Bosanski Novi, that there were the issuance of deadlines for the surrender of weapons and there were attacks on non-Serb areas there; I believe on the 10th and the 11th of November -- of May. I'm aware of -- in areas outside the Krajina, in Zvornik, in Bijeljina, that there had been military operations. And then there had also been takeovers which -- which may not necessarily have involved direct military actions, in terms of combat. And I know that that had happened in Prijedor, in Kljuc prior to this Assembly session in the Krajina. So there are examples, I think, that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus your attention, Mr. Brown, on the role of Serbian Territorial Defence units in the securing of territory in the implementation of the strategic objectives prior to their public announcement at the 16th Assembly Session. First of all, if I could direct your attention to an exhibit which is found in tab 45, which is the 14th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. This is an extract. That session was held on the 27th of March, 1992, in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am -- Dr. Karadzic is identified as the speaker at the bottom of page 22, and I am going to refer Mr. Brown to a passage that is found on 23, starting a little bit below halfway. It starts with the words "they can attempt."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This passage deals with the Territorial Defence, Mr. Brown. It says, "They can attempt to intimidate the Serbs here and there in Gorazde. They can kill someone in Brod. But they can never incorporate Serbian areas into their state or conquer them because they do not possess the forces required for the extensive territory held by the Serbs." Karadzic goes on to say, "We know that our people have armed themselves. We don't know the various ways and means by which this was done, but we do know that the people have enough weapons. I must say, however, that we do not have paramilitary units." "When you" -- he's -- now it's Karadzic talking to the members of the Assembly. "When you return to your municipalities, especially the newly formed municipalities, I ask you to do what you are required and entitled to do under the law. The moment you arrive in your municipality, you must urgently establish Crisis Staffs. You must try to organise the people so they can defend themselves. Find a number of reserve officers for those staffs and have them register everyone who owns weapons, as well as units. They should organise Territorial Defence, and if the JNA is there, they must be placed under its command. If they are not, let them be placed under the command of reserve officers." Now, let me also refer you, Mr. Brown, to the report on the army; then I'm going to invite your comment. On page 10 on the report on the army, which is, again, tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring Mr. Brown to the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that paragraph, it reads, "The command and" -- "The control Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and command function in the army framework of the establishment of the army of the Republika Srpska developed in two stages. First, from the 1st of April to 15 June 1992; and the second from that date until today. An important development in the first period was the self-organising and municipal" -- "of municipal and other regional units on the basis of Territorial Defence units under the political and patriotic influence of the Serbian Democratic Party. These units provided protection for the Serbian people against the Muslim and Croat forces, which were growing and becoming even more brutal. These units usually secured and liberated their municipality within their borders and stopped at that." Now, Mr. Brown, can I invite your comment on those two passages I've read to you, specifically focussing your attention on the development of Serb TOs and what role they had in achieving or attempting to achieve the strategic objectives that had -- were to be announced in a period later.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem that there is a relationship between both documents and there are other documents - I know of one in mid-April - which formally established the Serbian TO. I'm aware of the TO being involved in the takeover of authority in a number of Krajina municipalities in April and in the period before the 12th of May and the formal establishment of the army on the 12th of May. There is other references in the combat analysis report in 1993 saying that there was this two-phase: Phase 1, where there was Territorial Defence before the army was established, and then when the army was established, these Territorial Defence units being absorbed in. And I think there's a reference on page 69 of the army report which echoes that earlier comment, saying that during that first phase they failed to secure some of the strategic objectives. But I do know that they were able to take control of municipalities, some municipalities in the Krajina, and that some of that involved operations and joint operations with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So while they were able -- well, let me let the translators finish, first of all. While they were able, Mr. Brown, to achieve part of this realisation of the strategic objectives announced on this 16th Session, you said they couldn't achieve them all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they say themselves in the 1993 document, and I'd actually maybe draw your attention, also, to something that Mr. Krajisnik said at the 16th Assembly Session when the army was established. They passed a decision formally establishing the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you're looking for that passage, Mr. Brown, may I direct Your Honours' attention to the report on the army, page 69. Mr. Brown referred to it. It is passages that are found on page 69, starting with the paragraph that reads, "At the same time in the territory of the Republika Srpska ...." It's about the second paragraph down. And following down two paragraphs, which indicate that "The Territorial Defence units failed to achieve the main strategic objectives." And then in the passage that follows, it identifies -- the army report identifies which strategic objectives the Territorial Defence units failed to achieve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 51 of the translation of the 12th of May session, Mr. Krajisnik says, "We are at war, and it will be possible to solve this thing with Muslims and Croats only by war. And the politics will be instrumental in bringing it to an end. I do not know whether I have encompassed everything, but before we conclude, I would like to ask that we adopt and let us not compete/to see/who is the greater Serb. If it were up for election, no one in this hall is a greater one than me, but it will be the rational Serbs who are leading the Serbian people. Please, if we acquire these territories which we agree on and have conceived of today, plus the corridor we will get up there, we have done this generation -- we will have done -- this generation will have done so much for the Serbian people that this debt will be impossible to repay. What will really happen in reality? We will leave that to time. But it will be easier to achieve this now once we establish the Serbian army which we could have done earlier." And this may also be an indication that the objectives would have been easier to achieve or will be easier to achieve now that they have formed the army, rather than relying on what they had prior to that, which was the Serbian TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, throughout the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I apologise for interrupting. You have quoted from the report of the army the sentence [In English] : "They failed to achieve these strategics objectives," [Interpretation] and so on. Could the witness tell us why this territorial force could not achieve their principal objectives. What were the reasons? Was there resistance that existed? Could he answer this question, please? Why did the Territorial Defence, this territorial force, why did they fail in their attempts, or why did they not achieve their objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they had achieved some of them. They had managed to secure some territory. Dr. Karadzic talked about Sarajevo, for example, being encircled, that some of the municipalities had been taken over with their assistance and with their help. But in relation to, say, the corridor, maybe they were just not strong enough, maybe they were not - - not as well equipped, and it would have required the assistance of the equipment, the numbers, and the command and control and support processes that came with the JNA once it transitioned into the VRS. I don't know if they could have achieved the goals, you know, if they'd continued, but it might have taken an awful lot longer. But I think these are some of the reasons. It would have been easier to achieve it if they had had all the support, all the heavy weapons, all the artillery, the communications that came with the JNA when it transitioned into the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, in this period before the strategic objectives were announced at the 16th Session, did the documentation that you reviewed show that the Territorial Defence units worked in conjunction with SDS political bodies and in conjunction with the JNA to attempt to and actually implement parts of the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of the documentation I saw included references to joint operations between the JNA and the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, Mr. Brown, to --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Actually, before we move on to the next question, "Yes, some of the documentation included references," I think it would be useful for the Trial Chamber to know precisely what --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's where I was going before I was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm very pleased to hear that because I was afraid that we were moving on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood that Mr. Harmon would have an idea on what the witness might have in mind and was taking us to those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we first of all take a look at the document in tab 46. This is a military secret; it is from the command of the 5th Corps, the JNA unit. It is dated the 1st of April. It is addressed to the command of the 10th Partizan Division, and it is a -- it's an order, an order that is signed by the commander, General Talic. And if I can direct your attention first to the -- and affirm this for me, first of all, Mr. Brown: This is an order that relates to the elements under General Talic's control coming from Croatia into Bosnia at this point in time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The 6th Partizan Brigade was currently -- or at that time had been in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And was moving back from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to have you read part of his order and have you comment on it. It is found in the middle of -- a little bit below the middle of page one. General Talic orders, "Establish full cooperation with the organs of government in Sanski Most municipality and collaboration with TO and police units." Can I invite your brief comments on that.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's somewhat self-evident from the order. He's ordering his -- his subordinate brigade to go into Sanski Most and establish cooperation, full cooperation, with the organs in Sanski Most, and that is indeed what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me refer you to tab 47, again staying on this -- this theme, if you will, of the cooperation between Territorial Defence units and the JNA and SDS prior to the announcement of the strategic objectives. This next document in tab 47 is from the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's dated the 16th of April, and it is addressed to the governments of the Autonomous Region of essentially Krajina and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to all municipal -- to all Serbian municipalities. And it is signed by the National Defence minister, Bogdan Subotic. And this is a decision that was taken by the Ministry of Defence declaring a mobilisation, which we can see on the top of page 2, calling for a general mobilisation. And could you comment on the last paragraph in that document, "In the preparation for training and deployment of the TO units, effect cooperation with JNA units and, where possible, establish unified command."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, this seems to be self-evident that they are establishing the TO; they're mobilising the TO. And here in that section, they are instructing that there should be effective cooperation with the JNA units and where they can, establish a unified command in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if we can turn to the next exhibit, which is tab 48. Mr. Brown, this is a Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most. It's conclusions, and it is the conclusions of a meeting that took place on the 28th of April, a few weeks before the announcement of the strategic objectives -- two weeks before the announcement of the strategic objectives. And if I can refer you to the last item that reads, "That the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most meet with the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade, Colonel Basara, and start regulating the relationship between the Armed Forces of the Serbian Territorial Defence in the Yugoslav Army." I invite your comments.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would seem to indicate that the previous instructions -- well, firstly, that a Serbian Territorial Defence had been established in Sanski Most; that the 6th Brigade had arrived in Sanski Most, which it had done. Colonel Basara was the commander of the 6th Brigade. And that General Talic's order to ensure cooperation with the TO and the Subotic instruction, saying that there should be cooperation with the JNA, was, in fact, being -- were, in fact, being followed, and that in Sanski Most the Krajina Brigade and the TO were going to meet to regulate the relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the report on the army, one sees references to the term "liberating," "liberating territory." Mr. Brown, what does "liberating territory" mean in the context of the army report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that "liberating" meant taking over the levers of power in a territory, deploying where necessary military forces in order to do that or to assist in that, taking over complete control of that territory, deemed by, in this case, the Serbs as territory they wanted to control. I think that's what "liberating" -- "liberating" meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it from one of your earlier answers that the 6th Partizan Brigade was later renamed in the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. It was later renamed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then if we could turn to the document in tab 49. Mr. Brown, again on the issue of cooperation, this is a document that is dated the 11th of May, which is one day before the announcement of the strategic objectives. It is from the 5th Corps command. It is to the command of the 6th Brigade of the 10th Partizan Division, and it is from General Talic. And at the bottom of that document, it says, "I take this opportunity to pay tribute to and congratulate all the soldiers of the brigade and you personally for the successfully completed task of liberating the town of Bosanska Krupa." Now, Mr. Brown, can you comment on that particular paragraph, and can you tell the Judges, based on what you have seen in the documentation that you've reviewed, what happened in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same brigade that was in Sanski Most, and it deployed a component of that brigade to assist in -- in the takeover of Krupa. And General Talic here is congratulating the commander and the brigade for liberating, and if I -- liberating Bosanska Krupa. And if I take you back to what Miroslav Vjestica said had happened in Bosanska Krupa, clearly it had happened prior to the 12th of May in the 16th Assembly Session. That may give you an indication of what "liberating" meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to tab 50. Tab 50 is a Minister of the Interior Public Security Station sector report from the Municipality of Bosanski Novi, and it is a report that was prepared pursuant to a decision of the Ministry of National Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the decision of the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in association with the Bosanski Novi municipality Territorial Defence headquarters and with representatives of organs of the government. That's the -- that's why this report was prepared. And under the first subpart of this, "Reception centres in Bosanski Novi," the first paragraph, there is a reference, and I'd like to read this reference to you. It says, "However" -- it's about mid- paragraph. "However, these activities did not have the desired effect on the voluntary relinquishment of arms. And apart from that, during the night of 10 May 1992 in the village of Blagaj Rijeka," according to the report, "of a military police patrol an attack was mounted upon it. These events provoked a series of attacks on the areas and villages with majority Muslim population. Thus, on the 24th of May, 1992, the entire population from the villages in the area of Dolina Japra was accommodated in the central part of Blagaj Rijeka." Now, there is reference in this report to cooperation between the JNA and the Territorial Defence units participating in those attacks before the announcement of the strategic objectives. Mr. Brown, can you -- based on the documentation that you saw, can you tell us what happened in the area of the Japra Valley in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe from that document that most of the Muslim population, if not all of the Muslim population, was -- was moved out or left. I'd also draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, is my recollection correct that we had quite some evidence on what happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying very quickly to put it into context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't intend to explore it. We've heard, as I recall, considerable evidence on this municipality.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just maybe quickly draw your attention as well to, again, Miroslav Vjestica, in his statement at the 16th Assembly Session, indicated that he had visited Novi around this time and he made mention that the area had been sealed off, an ultimatum had been issued, and that he -- he believed that -- that there was a issue of weapon deadlines and the surrender of weapons. So he clearly had visited that area himself and -- and articulated that at the 16th Assembly Session. And there are a couple of other references in this police document. For example, at the top, the reference 1/92 of the 16th of April is the Bogdan Subotic instruction which we've just seen. And the -- there was a -- also a decision, I think, on the 4th or 5th of May from the Autonomous Region of Krajina which referenced the Bogdan Subotic instruction that set these deadlines for the illegal -- to the handover of illegally-held weapons. So there's a chain that runs from the Ministry of the Interior -- the Bogdan Subotic Ministry of Defence instruction and the establishment of the TO and the mobilisation through the ARK down to the municipality, and using those references as reasons, as well as the fact that they referenced that they were -- there was an attack on a military police patrol, but those were the reasons why they were carrying out these operations. So there is a -- there is a relationship between the regional level, the republic level, and this municipality attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if we could turn to tab 52, and we will conclude with the topic of these Territorial Defence units before the break. Tab 52 is a 1st Krajina Corps strictly confidential proposal that went to the Main Staff of the army. It is dated the 27th of May, 1992, which is 15 days after the strategic objectives were announced, and this is a proposal that in part proposes, Mr. Brown, that the Territorial Defence units be incorporated into the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that had actually also been discussed at the 12th of May Assembly session, I have to say, that the TO should be integrated into the VRS. General Talic indicated in his corps on the 27th of May which TOs he felt should be integrated into his corps, and that is, in fact, what happened. They generally became known as light brigades. So most often if you see the reference to a "light brigade," or a "light infantry brigade," quite often that was formed from the Serb TO or the TO that was present prior to the establishment of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to page 4 and page 5, and very quickly, Mr. Brown, just guide the Court through subpart 4, which is at the bottom of page 4, all the way through the -- part 4, if you will. It ends on about a third of the way up on page 5.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part on -- or the first part of page -- of section 4 on page 4, the very last few lines, are the -- were the areas that General Talic believed that he could form light brigades from existing TO units. He then suggests how these units should be grouped, and then he makes a note that the current commanders of municipal TO defence staffs would be commanders of light infantry brigades. And so he -- and then he talks about the rough strength of these light infantry brigades. And in many cases, I believe - I'm not quite so sure about Prijedor - but I think for many of the other ones these light infantry brigades did -- did become formed units of the Krajina Corps and operated under General Talic's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- is this the appropriate time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's an appropriate time for a break. Mr. Harmon, we'll have a break until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Harmon, in view of scheduling, the Chamber thought it wise to have some escapes, if need would be. Of course, the Chamber hopes that we do not need escapes. The escapes would be to continue tomorrow for one more half hour, and if that would not do - I said one more -- one half hour more, I should say. I think that's proper English. If that would not do, I was informed that if we would need one or two hours in the morning of Thursday, although the Chamber considered Thursday sacrosanct, that it would not meet insurmountable objections by the Defence. And one of the other escape modes would be the morning of next week Thursday. That would be the day of the Plenary, but the Chamber finds it very important to see whether we can meet the 22nd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the 22nd of July, I will be on a different continent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 21st, then, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be on a different continent on the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the 20th. Let me just -- I think I was talking about the 21st, but if I'm not mistaken ... So it's good to know that on the 20th and the 22nd you'll be on another continent, so we could sit on the 21st, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have colleagues that will be sitting with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. These are just escape routes, but that the parties are informed where the escape lanes are. And for next Thursday, I'd like to know very much whether the parties would think we would need, next Thursday, a couple of hours in the morning. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have spoken with Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- in respect of the possibility of sitting on this Thursday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- it being designated earlier as a free day. And Mr. Stewart has informed me that he has no objection in that situation, should it arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but for -- it's not only whether we are willing, but the Registry has to organise it all with teams of interpreters, et cetera. So therefore I would also very much like to know not whether we could sit but whether we would need those hours to sit. That depends on the time you'd still need, Mr. Harmon, and the time the Defence would need and the time the Judges would need. Could you give us any impression?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I can reserve that till the end of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although Madam Registrar would have loved to know it by now because now she can take action; at the end of this session, she can't take any action.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, I will need the rest of this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The rest of this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will try to finish earlier, but the rest of this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, would you need more than one day?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, on current indications, yes, I would need more than one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One day and half an hour would not be ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, of course, that would be a day, of course, for my cross-examination, leaving alone, of course, questions of re- examination and additional questions from Your Honours and, of course the question of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- cross-examination by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would rather say additional questions by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Yes. So in that regard, Your Honour, I can indicate I am more than happy to proceed on Thursday, be it if we're talking about this week Thursday or in addition next week Thursday, as well. That would be fine from my perspective, I can indicate. The other question is: I was -- I was also asked if I was prepared to agree to sitting one hour earlier tomorrow, which I agreed I was -- I was happy to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether we can combine the one hour earlier and the half an hour. That's not possible, I hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But that's where I stand, Your Honour. I'm in Your Honours' hands in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can -- it seems to me quite clear that the time available for this witness, if we were to end by close of play Wednesday, would not be sufficient to deal with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And so therefore it's a question of logistics, in terms of the remaining time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I think the matter is clear enough, and let's give the opportunity to Mr. Harmon to see whether he succeeds in finishing earlier than 7.00. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to be proceeding on the topic of paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, during the period before the announcement of the strategic objectives, were Serb paramilitary forces used in part to liberate territories sought by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, rather than the question being asked in this leading form, the -- I would submit the evidence should be elicited from the witness by means of a -- an open question. I mean, this is an important question, and it -- and it deserves a non-leading approach, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- Mr. Harmon, although I sometimes find that Ms. Loukas is objecting to leading too early, she's not here. Could we ask the witness first to tell us about the involvement of the paramilitaries in -- paramilitary forces, if any, in the military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In total, Your Honour? Before and after the strategic objective or ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, in military operations by armed forces of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of some documentation that highlights that paramilitary units -- some paramilitary units were involved in -- in operations by -- by Bosnian Serb, TO, and JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What kind of operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm aware of Arkan in Zvornik and Bijeljina. I'm aware of the integration of the Serbian defence force into the Serbian TO - - or a document that highlights the integration of the Serbian defence force, SOS, into the Sanski Most TO. I'm aware of the activities of Veljko Milankovic, a paramilitary leader who came from Prnjavor and had a group that operated in -- both in Croatia in 1991 and was integrated into the VRS 1st Krajina Corps in 1992, and that unit was involved in operations. I'm aware of some paramilitary groups that operated in Prijedor, Cigo's group, Zolja's group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the Chamber has heard quite some evidence on taking military control of Serbian municipalities. Were they involved in that type of operations, as well? Or were the examples you gave in relation to such type of operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm aware of in Prijedor those groups, Cigo's group, being part of the 43rd Motorised Brigade, which took part in the attacks in Prijedor in May 1992. The reference to the SOS in Sanski Most, I think the document is late April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We heard some evidence on the SOS in Sanski Most. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn to the item in tab 53. This, Mr. Brown, is a conclusion of a Crisis Staff of Sanski Most meeting that was held on the 21st and the 22nd of April, 1992. It is dated the 22nd of April, 1992. And point 6 in that group reads as follows: "The Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most hereby adopts the conclusion that the Serbian defence forces are to be placed at the disposal of the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence and engaged as a special unit of the Serbian Territorial Defence." The Serbian defence forces: what can you tell the Court about them? Very briefly, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the Serbian defence forces, or SOS, had been involved in blockading Banja Luka in April, early April 1992. And I would assume that here they are being integrated into the TO according to this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could we turn, then, Mr. Brown, to paragraph -- tab 54. This, Mr. Brown, is from the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is a document that was distributed, as one can see on page 6, to, among others, the 1st Krajina Corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps, the Eastern Bosnia Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and the Herzegovina Corps, and to the president of the SRBiH Presidency, the Prime Minister of the SRBiH, and the commander of the Main Staff. And it's a report that was prepared on the 28th of July, 1992 on paramilitary formations that were operating in the Serbian Republic of BH. Can you tell us, Mr. Brown, what this document is in respect of, that report. What are the salient features of this report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fairly lengthy document outlines a number of issues. It -- it highlights that -- well, as it's entitled, it's a report on paramilitary formations in the territory of the SRBH, and outlines that they are a feature of the -- of the war, and it lists the characteristics and the characteristics are, you know, the unpleasant characteristics, low moral qualities, looting, robbing, mass murder; I think they use the phrase "genocidal element of the Serbian people." So it presents them in a very critical way. It then outlines later in the document, from around about page 3, I think, some of the various groups, that they -- they categorise as paramilitaries, and it lists a number of them in various locations throughout SRBiH, saying where they work, what they may have done, and where they are now. Some of those groups highlighted in here have -- appear already to have been integrated into the VRS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, let me stop you right there. A list of groups that you're talking about, it starts on, I think, page 3 and it carries over until page 5. Can you identify the groups that were operating within the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 3, third paragraph from the bottom indicates a group, a Serbian -- a Serbian Radical Party group in Banja Luka. The next paragraph indicates a group in Sipovo. In the following page, page 4, the second -- or, sorry, the group headed by Zoran Barisic, that brigade was highlighted -- the 19th Brigade was part of Talic's corps, and it would seem to have been integrated by then. Mrkonjic Grad is within General Talic's corps; that's the next paragraph down. There's a -- a reference -- the following paragraph is a revival of paramilitary formations in the area of Kljuc. That was in General Talic's zone. The next paragraph down, the group of 13 members held -- headed by Zeljko Skrbic in the zone of the 1st Krajina Brigade of the 30th Division; that was in General Talic's corps. The proclaimed groups in Prijedor, Cigo's group, Zolja's group, that was -- they were in General Talic's corps, and they were actually part of the 43rd Brigade, which was one of General Talic's units. The following one, Mile Janjatovic in Bosanska Gradiska, that was in General Talic's corps. The detachment of Veljko Milankovic from Prnjavor, that was in General Talic's corps. And Milankovic was, in fact, it says here, formally under command of the 1 KK. There's the reference to the Serbian defence forces in Banja Luka. That was in General Talic's corps. On page 5, Teslic was in General Talic's corps, and the Teslic area fell under his authority. I think -- I think those are the main ones there which ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I refer you down to -- no, strike that. Okay. Now, what was the role, Mr. Brown, of these paramilitary units that are identified in this document in achieving strategic objectives that have been identified by the Bosnian Serb Assembly? What role did they play in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would object to approaching it with this assumption in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I think the question should be whether they did play any role in that respect and what, if any, that role would be. Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't tell you for each of these paramilitary groups exactly what they did. It is -- it is not -- I have not necessarily come across material that would indicate every single issue that they -- they were involved in. But what I would say is that some of them were integrated into the 1st Krajina Corps. This document highlights that some of them were already working in the 1st Krajina Corps. I know that the units in Prijedor were formally part of General Talic's brigade that actively took part in attacks on Kozarac, Hambarine, and other areas in Prijedor. I know that Veljko Milenkovic, who is referenced in this report, took part in -- well, he came from Prnjavor (Milankovic) and actually had been active in the 5th Corps, but was also involved in -- directly in combat operations in the Corridor in June 1992 as a unit that took part in that -- in that wider operation. So in some of these units, I would argue that they were integrated into the VRS and they took part in -- in combat operations of the -- of the 1st Krajina Corps, but I -- I cannot say for -- for all of them, because I -- I have not looked at -- in detail at all of them. But some of them I do know. And actually the document itself is -- is about integrating these units into the VRS, bringing them under control of the army. The -- the document is very critical in the first couple of pages about what these paramilitaries have done and are capable of doing.
