And, you know, they call it the genocidal element of the Serb -- the Serbian people, but when you get to the end, page 6, the instruction is that they are -- they are -- they're causing difficulties because they diminish the trust in the government and they discourage the fighting of other -- of the army, and they -- they instruct that every armed Serb group must be placed under the command of the army, and if they don't, then they can be disbanded and legal measures taken. But what they don't do in this document is upfront say that here we have a group of people who are the genocidal element; these people should be prosecuted. That should be -- but it would seem to me what they're doing here is bringing the type of people that you would least want to have in a military, which are people who loot, who don't fight, who are war profiteers, and who have clearly committed crimes. And the implication here is that these people will be tolerated as long as they're brought within the legal framework of the army, and this is why I think this document is of -- is of some importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I put a question in this respect directly related to your answer: If they say the presence and activity negatively affect the Serbian people in two ways, is it logical to assume that once they're subordinated, that one would expect them to continue exactly the same activities? I mean, that would not help anyone out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I could illuminate that by an example. Veljko Milankovic was highlighted in late 1991. He is referenced in this document. He is highlighted in 1991 as being a man who had a criminal record and whose group was causing problems. His group was attached to the 5th Corps and continued to cause problems, and I think there are highlights of looting. This document highlights that he is still engaged in that process, yet he is formally under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. And I would argue in his case that -- you know, that this is a man who had a previous record; he was employed in Croatia; he conducted that -- that activity; he continued to cause problems when he was in the VRS, and yet he remained in the VRS, being given orders to go to Knin in late 1992 -- late 1993, where he was wounded and later died. So from a military perspective and from an ex-military officer, I have to go back to this issue of these people would be the least likely -- you know, the least -- the people you would last want to have in -- in a military with that clear pattern and -- and clear background, and yet this document to me seems to be saying that they will be tolerated as long as they're brought within the formal structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at the same time, if you would get them into the normal army structures it would not help in any way, since they would even perhaps more diminish the trust in the government than being part of the official army; and, second, if they would continue to act as they did before, would they any less discourage the fighting [inaudible] of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army members? I try to understand how, if they would continue to act as they did, how this would change anything in view of the concerns expressed on page 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only imagine that they felt that if they were in there that, you know, they were part of a formal structure and therefore they could somehow maybe control them. But -- but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would then express a wish to end the misbehaviour of these paramilitary units; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say whether that is what -- it -- it may well be one of the reasons that, this was -- seems as a problem, and that one way was to bring them in, and they felt that -- that might be able to control them. But it -- it would strike me as being -- that having already highlighted what these people had been capable of doing, that what they're not saying is the very thing that should happen, which is that these people should be disarmed and prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I can only assume that they didn't want to do that because they also may have, you know, been against their wider interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to -- do you know anything about the origin of these paramilitaries? How did they appear? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I can't tell you the details. I haven't studied each group in -- in -- as an individual. I am aware that they -- they became present, many from -- actually the war in Croatia, as well, helped; Milankovic, you know, being an example of that. But I don't think I can explain all of them. I haven't studied them in-depth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we, then, say that this happened spontaneously, that there was no initiative by certain individuals? Did they correspond to a need that was expressed by a certain authority? How would you account for their being about -- for their appearance on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One explanation, maybe, if I draw you back to that document, one of the earlier documents which I flagged up, which was a distribution of weapons by the JNA and the SDS. Clearly the arming had occurred. There are some references, I believe, in this document - I'd like to go over it a little bit later - which link them to some political affiliations, political parties. I think there's references, even though they say at the beginning they're not linked to the SDS, I think there are a couple of references from the individual groups themselves that talk about SDS relationships. There are political parties referenced in the document, and -- and that might be a way when -- you know, as a means of them being armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I direct your attention, Mr. Brown, you said "SDS." If you turn to page 3, to the municipality of Sipovo. Do you see that reference? The second paragraph from the bottom of page 3. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there's another reference here, as well, on page 4, to -- in a different municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrkonjic Grad, maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's found at the top of page 4, third paragraph -- second paragraph down: "SDS members in the area of Mrkonjic Grad." Can you comment on those references?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they would seem to indicate that there was this relationship with the SDS and that they had been -- and certainly Sipovo had been formed under the leadership of -- or backed by SDS leaders, and the SDS had tried to form one in Mrkonjic Grad. So this document would seem to say that there is a relationship there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, you were talking about disarming these groups. By and large or generally speaking, if you know, how large were these groups? Are we talking thousands of men? Are we talking hundreds of men?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this report itself mentions, I think -- I think it says there -- they tend to be in groups of about 30 to 40 men, and I think at this time they said there were about 60 groups working in the BiH. So that would be under 1.000, maybe, in total, under 2.000. But not, in comparison to the VRS, somewhat --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We had -- we took --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- significantly smaller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We took a look at the earlier document, the report on the army. I started out this afternoon by identifying a portion that showed the number -- the numerical strength of the army in respect of the paramilitaries. Did the army, in your opinion, have the capacity to suppress all of those paramilitary groups that are identified?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. If the army had been capable of conducting the large-scale military operations that it did in some places in Bosnia, like the Corridor, in Sarajevo, and other places, with its size alone, in comparison with these other paramilitary, I would argue that yes, they could quite easily have dealt with this issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, in the first paragraph of this document, it identifies a number of formations: Arkan's men, Seselj's men, Dragan's -- Captain Dragan's commandos and the like. You earlier in your testimony referenced Bijeljina. And do you know in -- in -- the events in Bijeljina occurred in -- actually, do you know when the events in Bijeljina occurred?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe Bijeljina was -- the events occurred in the last few days of March and first few days of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if any paramilitary formations were involved in the events in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Arkan's paramilitaries were involved in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So by late March in Bijeljina, there was reference to -- there was an awareness of paramilitary activities and conduct. And this document is dated the 28th of July, almost four months later. I have two questions for you. One is, By the 28th of July, 1992 in the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, what -- can you give us a summary of what had happened in respect of the strategic objectives and the implication of the strategic objectives in the 1st Krajina Corps by the 28th of July, 1992? Just a general overview.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much of the territory that encompassed the 1 Krajina Corps's area of responsibility had been under control of the corps. They had conducted attacks in many of the municipalities: Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, Kotor Varos. It -- and they had control of -- of most of their zone. They had conducted a large-scale operation in the Corridor, along with another corps and -- and other elements, and had taken control of the Corridor by then. And they had -- the small section that they did have on the Una River was also under their control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of the non-Serb population, what had happened to the non-Serb population in the area of the 1 KK by the 28th of July, 1992? Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that is actually a question that the witness can't answer. His report is based on his reading and assimilation of various documents. What occurred in the area of the 1 KK, as indicated by Mr. Harmon, is actually the -- the matter -- one of the matters that Your Honours must decide and certainly someone, Your Honour, who was not there and is merely analysing the documents cannot glean what occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I disagree with counsel. This report that has been prepared by Mr. Brown addresses specifically that issue. And the documents that he used to base his report in his conclusions on address those very issues of resettlement. There's a section in Mr. Brown's report on the resettlement, the role of the JNA, the role of the VRS in those events, the role of the police, so I think Mr. Brown is perfectly capable of answering that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the witness, when asked about certain events, very often started his answer by saying "on the basis of the documents, I found that." Let's hear his answer and see whether he certainly has personal knowledge of matters or whether he still relies on documents he studied.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Loukas, please. Microphone for Ms. Loukas, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let's listen to his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the documentation I have reviewed, there are references to expulsion, removal, resettlement, people moving out, people - - authorities who should work harder at this. There are documents indicating numbers of people had moved out. There are references to people being moved to detention centres, being moved to detention centres from other detention centres, and there are references of people being moved out of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I have concluded this portion of the examination on paramilitaries if Your Honours have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least, I have one question which -- the document you're dealing with at this moment confuses me a bit. On the top of page 4, where I always thought that Arkan was Zeljko Raznjatovic, suddenly another Arkan appears, which is new to me. Could the witness help me out, because Mr. Zoran Barisic is here, given the name Arkan, and apart from that, I have some difficulties to understand the whole paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only imagine that he's used that -- that name. It's not relating to the Arkan who took over Bijeljina. It's a different one. And he may just have decided to use the same name or -- or -- it was a name that was given to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is what you think might be the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can only assume that from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's clear, then. Then it says, "But the commander of the 19th Brigade has received constant treats from both the former and the present group." I have not seen a former and a present group, apart from what treats are supposed to mean here or would it be threats or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would imagine it's probably a misspelling and it's "threats."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it, Mr. Harmon, that you'll -- and "former and present group," is ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's unclear whether -- it's not too clear from this what exactly he means, whether he's -- you know, he was part of a previous group before he joined the 19th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this is speculation, just as the other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll check the translation. On the B/C/S, it's page 4 of the B/C/S. I'll have that checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I'm not asking you for a new translation to be provided. If it's a mistake, we could correct it and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final -- actually, I have one final question, Mr. Brown. Are you aware that after some of these paramilitary groups were entered -- integrated into the VRS that they continued to commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know of the groups in Prijedor that -- that continued to do that. And I know that Milankovic caused some significant problems at the VRS. In fact, they mentioned that he's involved in looting, I think, and he's -- he's already in the VRS by then, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to what happened to those people who were integrated into the VRS who continued to commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Milankovic remained in the VRS until he was wounded in the Knin. He was sent to the Knin by Talic in, I believe, February 1993. He was wounded there and later died in -- in the military hospital in Belgrade. Cigo, his -- his unit remained, I believe, in Prijedor between the 43rd Brigade and another brigade that was based in Prijedor. I don't think he -- anything happened to him through the war. Zoran Karlica who was another one in the 43rd Brigade, I believe, was -- was killed during the operations in -- in Prijedor. But I know certainly of Cigo and -- and Milankovic. They stayed in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to change the subject, Mr. Brown. I'd like to go to the -- come back to the 16th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly and ask you, Mr. Brown, if you know how those strategic objectives were disseminated, disseminated to both the military units in the 1 KK and to the civil structures, if you know that based on the information you have reviewed.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly the dissemination of the -- at the Assembly session itself, when Mr. Karadzic announced the goals and -- and spoke to the delegates there as a dissemination process, Ratko Mladic was there, General Talic was there. You know, the -- the whole announcement itself was a dissemination process. So that is one. And I'm assuming that the Assembly sessions were a vehicle whereby that could be disseminated down the political chain. I'm aware from documentation that there are references soon after the announcement of the goals in documents that would relate to the goals of our struggle, the announcements of the goals in one document. The directives clearly indicate a dissemination of the goals and a knowledge and understanding. So there -- there seem to be very much a dissemination of those goals down to the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to tab 55. This is a document that is an excerpt from the minutes of a tape recording of the RS National Assembly, the 27th Session that was held on the 3rd of April, 1993. I'm not sure if this has been admitted as an exhibit this. This is a document provided by Mr. Krajisnik earlier. Now, let me draw the Court's attention to page 7 of this document, the portion under the word "chairman," which is Mr. Krajisnik, and let me quote a portion of this to you and get your reaction. I'm reading from -- starting at the fifth line down from the word "chairman." "Why are so many people attending Assembly sessions? Why are some people sitting at the rear? Presidents of Executive Boards of municipalities and presidents of local SDS branches come along, et cetera. It is because it has a special significance in war. That is the best way to keep our people aware of what is going on. We have seen that people were leaving the Assembly sessions with a clear vision of what they were supposed to do." And it goes on, and a few lines down it says, "And believe me, once our opinions are crystal clear, then it is way easier to work in the field." Can you comment? You were talking about dissemination of information, and I'm talking about the dissemination of the strategic objectives on -- can you comment on this passage?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem to state the importance of the Assembly sessions in disseminating the message that they wanted down and that people would leave with a clear understanding of what they were supposed to do. So it's not just a dissemination of -- of a message but -- but what people were actually meant to do with that message.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'd like to take you through a series of documents showing the dissemination of these strategic objectives. If we could start with the document that is found on tab 56. And this document is from the command of the 1st Partizan Brigade. It is dated the 14th of May, which is two days after the strategic objectives were announced. It's a meeting with the presidents of municipalities in the zone of responsibility of the division. And it identifies in Part 4 on page 1, it discusses a discussion on -- and proposals -- I'm sorry, this is the agenda: Discussion and proposals for future cooperation with JNA units in the domains of securing territory and treatment of soldiers (unit commanders) in the area of Serbian Krajina. And then it identifies the people who are present. And very briefly, Mr. Brown, can you identify the military people who are present, what their roles were.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Galic was the commander of the 30th Division, which was a subordinate formation of General Talic and part of the 1st Krajina Corps. Colonel Basara, we've mentioned before; he was a brigade commander, and his brigade -- it says "Partizan Brigade," it was later called the Krajina Brigade. It was a subordinate -- no, it wasn't a subordinate, the 30th Division. It was a brigade operated under General Galic and it covered Sanski Most. Colonel Stevan Popovic [phoen] I think, was a staff soldier under General Galic, and then there's a reference of the TO staff commander, Major Bosko Lukic [phoen] from Kljuc. And then there are various -- various presidents of municipalities, and those municipalities were within the zone of the 30th Division. The stamp on the top of the document is from the command of the 1st Partizan Brigade. The 1st Partizan Brigade was a subordinate unit of the 30th Division. So I'm assuming that these minutes had been disseminated down from the 30th Division to the Partizan Division.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I direct your attention to page 3 of this document, referring to the second and third paragraphs in that document. Can you tell us about that, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Galic, from the minutes, is informing those present of what's happening in the various zones, so in terms of the various municipalities in his zone. And in Kljuc, they mention the partial takeover of power, the situation in the territory of Kljuc municipality is relatively calm. At the time of the takeover of power, units from the 9th Corps and the 5th Corps (a battalion of the 6th Partizan Brigade and the 3rd/1st" -- "3rd Battalion, 1st Partizan Brigade) were secure in Kljuc."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention, Mr. Brown, to page 3, and specifically in reference to the strategic objectives. What's happening?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Colonel Galic gave an overview of the municipalities, the president of Mrkonjic Grad municipality, Milan Nalija [phoen] presented the conclusions from the meeting held in Banja Luka, and bearing in mind this is two days after the 12th of May. And also what he discusses were the very issues that had been discussed at the 12th of May. I'm assuming he is referencing that conference that he presumably had attended. He talks about the formation of the army and he says here, "It was assessed that this army can occupy a large territory." And he talks about the strategic goals formulated at the meeting in Banja Luka, and he presents them, and he lists the strategic goals as articulated at the -- I mean, they're not exactly a verbatim word-for-word copy of what Radovan Karadzic says, but it's the same goals: separation, the Drina -- the Corridor, the Drina, borders on the Una and Neretva, Sarajevo must be divided -- and here he says "or razed to the ground" and examine the possibility of access to the sea. So he seems to be relaying those goals down within this forum, which includes the municipal leaders, the military commanders, and, as I say from the stamp on this document, it would seem that this had been disseminated further down the chain in the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, at the end of the document, Colonel Galic makes a proposal. And can you review and comment on the proposal that was made and ultimately adopted at this session, this meeting.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Galic, the first one is -- states, "Implement the decisions from the meeting in Banja Luka, but submit them to the commands of units and municipalities." He then talks about "all forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina should work towards the same goals." He also mentions war profiteering should be prevented. And he commends soldiers "for the combat results achieved so far." So he then -- these conclusions are unanimously adopted, presumed, by those who attended the meeting. He also notes that "meetings should be held every 15 days," and that "Municipal presidents" -- "Presidents of Municipal Assemblies," sorry, "should be responsible for this." So for me this document is of some interest in that it comes very quickly after the Assembly. It reflects or briefs the goals. It shows cooperation between the military and the civilian leadership. It stresses decisions that -- or conclusions that they should implement the decisions from the meeting in Banja Luka, that they should all have the same goals. These decisions are unanimously adopted by those present at the meeting, and that they should continue to have meetings afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, on the subject of dissemination, if we can turn -- on the subject of dissemination of the strategic objectives, if we can turn to tab 57, and very briefly, Mr. Brown, because we have a lot of exhibits to go through. This is a document dated the 21st of May, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is this -- is this the document that appears, Your Honours, in your tab 57, a document dated the 21st of May from the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's actually document 58, I think -- behind tab 58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 57 seems --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to be a 1st Krajina Corps command, 2nd of August, 1992, combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It should be 57, Your Honour. What -- maybe there's some confusion in these documents. Is 57 -- the document that appears in your 57, a document from the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 21st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Then if we could go to tab 9. It may have been placed in tab 9 of your binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This, Your Honour, should be a document from the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 21st of May, an order on general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Again, we're discussing dissemination. Can you briefly explain the significance of this document, which is dated nine days after the strategic objectives were announced.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I covered briefly this document yesterday, and I think, if I direct you to the section 6 on page 2, General Talic states here -- this is a general mobilisation order based on a Presidency decision of the previous day, and he outlines many -- many issues. But on section 6, he says, "Explain to conscripts as they arrive the goals of our struggle and brief them on the rights" -- "their duties and rights."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the distribution list at the end is quite extensive, from what I can see so far.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's the -- the various units and sub-units of the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn to tab 58 now. Just take a minute for the Judges to get control of the paper that's in front of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We gain experience, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring Your Honours to tab 58 in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document, Mr. Brown, that is from the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 21st of May, 1992, to the command. It is a document that -- you can see at the end, the distribution list, at the bottom of page 3 it's sent to all of the corps units, and it's been sent to them by -- this document has been prepared by the assistant commander for moral guidance, Colonel Vukelic. And I direct your attention, Mr. Brown, to the top paragraph at page 2, starting at the third line. It says, "The constituent Serbian people who live on or around 65 per cent of the area and represent more than 35 per cent of the population of BH must struggle for the complete separation from the Muslim and Croat peoples and form their own state." Can I invite you to comment on that, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would seem to echo very much the issue of separation and strategic goal number 1. This is a report that was written by the morale officer who went down to the corps and outlines the -- the view of the current conflict. I'd also like to draw your attention to the very end, where he says -- the very last sentence, actually, before the signature block on page 3: "Inform all members of the army of the Serbian Republic of BH about the contents of this report in the most suitable way." And it's handwritten on the back, "Sent to all corps units." I think the complete separation would seem to have some resonance with strategic goal number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these strategic goals, Mr. Brown, I want to focus on the subject of their being re-emphasised after the 16th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. And if we could turn first of all to the document that is found on -- in tab 59. This is a large document. On page 1, it identifies the document. A name is used in it. And this is a diary. The name is Colonel Novica Simic. Do you know who Colonel Novica Simic is?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the -- he initially was a JNA officer who served in the 1st Krajina Corps. But at this time, he -- he was the East Bosnia Corps commander. So he was a corps commander based in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I direct Your Honours' attention and your attention, Mr. Brown, to page 37 of this diary. This diary -- actually, we're going to be referring to pages 37 through 39. But this diary entry starts with the reference "A meeting with the RS Presidency," and it's dated September the 2nd. It identifies the participants in this meeting. And if we turn to page 38 of this meeting, it identifies the president of the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik, and what he talked about. And if you go to the bottom of this page, under "Strategic goals," as noted by Colonel Simic, it appears they are listed with the first goal -- the first goal is "the separation from the Muslims"; and then 2 is "corridors"; 3, "division of Sarajevo"; 4, "Drina Valley-Serbs"; "Border on the Neretva River," and 6, "exit to the sea." Mr. Brown, can I have your observations about the notations that are entered in this -- in Colonel Simic's diary.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would seem that at this meeting in September the strategic goals were still being put forward, re-emphasised at a -- at a high level, and this is the corps commander. And it's the same strategic goals as were articulated in May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if you'd get the next binder, binder 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn to tab 60. Mr. Brown, this is an excerpt from the Bosnian -- the 20th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which was held on the 14th and 15th of September, 1992, in Bijeljina, and if I can direct your attention and Your Honours' attention to page 3 of this excerpt. I'll quote the relevant passage, which is found on page 3, and I will be reading from the eleventh line down, where reference is to Mr. Krajisnik. And the speaker of this is Dr. Karadzic, as identified on page -- at the top of page 1. Dr. Karadzic says the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any problem?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I cannot follow because all the time a reference is made to the English version and the Prosecutor never mentions the B/C/S version of that same text, making it very hard for me to follow what's being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, it's difficult enough for us to find it regularly. Could we -- I'll also try to assist in locating the relevant B/C/S portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, Your Honour, this is in Cyrillic, and I can't read Cyrillic, so -- it is on the third -- it's on the third page of the English translation, and it mentions Mr. Krajisnik's name, so perhaps Mr. Krajisnik can easily find it. But I will read it, Your Honour, and in the process Mr. Krajisnik may be able to better locate the document, the passage that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've asked my case manager to assist Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that we are all working on a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I may read, Your Honour, then, this passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The passage that I'm going to read, as I say, I've identified its location and this is Dr. Karadzic speaking, and he says the following: "Mr. Krajisnik, Koljevic and myself were Visegrad yesterday and then in Rudo. The military leadership of the Cajnice Brigade was also in Rudo -- "

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. It just -- I think just to assist this process, it would be useful to have the ERN number in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can't read it, so I can give you the ERN numbers of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the ERN numbers are not in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The ERN number is 04226207. That's the -- on the first page. And it goes through 212. I'll start again, Your Honour, if I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Mr. Krajisnik, Koljevic and myself were in Visegrad yesterday and then in Rudo. The military leadership of the Cajnice Brigade was also in Rudo, and we talked about the fact that since the relieving of pressure on Gorazde the pressure on those municipalities has increased, so we'll have to increase pressure on Gorazde in order to relieve these municipalities. There will be another meeting of commanders tomorrow, and we think that together with them we will make some important decisions; namely, the Drina is of great strategic importance to us, that is, it is of the highest strategic importance. If the green transversal is to cut off along the Drina, then a Muslim Bosnia will lose significance." A few lines down, at the end of the paragraph, Dr. Karadzic continues and says, "We want to secure the Drina and all of the municipalities -- and all of our municipalities and all of our houses along the Drina. That way we will connect with the Eastern Sanski Corps." Now, Mr. Brown, if we go to tab 61. Go to tab 61, Mr. Brown. This is a document that is from the 1st -- from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, dated the 14th of September. It's from Colonel Vukelic, and it's a report on military consultations. And, in fact, as you can see in the first and second paragraphs, it is a report on consultations that were attended by, among others, General Mladic, General Talic, Major General Ninkovic, Colonel Bogdan Subotic, who was the Minister of Defence. And in the second paragraph, it says, "In addition to the commanders of units and institutions of the 1st Krajina Corps, consultations were attended by the presidents of 26 municipalities in the organs of the Minister of the Interior in our zone of responsibility." And in this document, it says two paragraphs down, "In his presentation, General Ratko Mladic described the overall political and military situation as very complex and demanded the absolute unity of all armed forces, political structures, and MUP organs, especially in carrying out our" -- "out operations and strategic tasks, the functioning of the government, and the prevention of war profiteering, which is a heavy burden on people's minds." Now, Mr. Brown, did you see throughout the documentation that you reviewed, the military documentation, a reiteration of the objectives, strategic objectives that had been announced on the 16th of -- at the 16th Session?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I -- I see -- I see that in a number of areas. We've covered that in some areas. I would like to draw your attention to that first document that you mentioned, about the Drina Valley, that being a strategic objective. That comes some six weeks before operational directive objective four came out, which tasked the Drina Corps to take control of those municipalities we talked about yesterday. It highlights, as well, that from -- from this document that Mr. Karadzic -- that you said Mr. Krajisnik and one other, Koljevic, were able to visit areas, speak to military commanders. There was going to be further meetings. The second document, clearly municipal leaders were being talked to by senior military commanders and re-emphasising the strategic tasks that were being set out. And that along with the directives and some of the other documentation would seem to indicate that the strategic objectives were -- were being re-emphasised and were important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, let's -- let's go from the reiteration of the objectives to the actual implementation of the objectives, and let me highlight some documents that are found in your report. In your report, in paragraphs 2.2 and 2.3, at pages 60 and 61, you describe combat operations as being two distinct types; they can be divided into two distinct but overlapping categories. One, a series of operations to seize and control and secure territory claimed by the Serbs; and in paragraph 2.3 of your report, you say the second category consisted of large-scale formal military operations directed by the Main Staff, and you describe two of those operations, Operation Corridor and Operation Vrbas, which dealt with Jajce. I don't want to dwell on Operation Corridor, Mr. Brown, but can you very briefly describe what its purpose and objective was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this Operation Corridor, Your Honour is described in Mr. Brown's report at paragraph 2.212 to 2.217. We're not going to emphasise --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're not going to spend a lot of time on Operation Corridor, Mr. Brown, but can you just briefly describe to the Judges what is that operation was?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Corridor was an operation, as its name would suggest, to open up a corridor between the -- the Krajina, as articulated by Radovan Karadzic in strategic goal number 2. The sequence very briefly would seem to be the -- possibly the issue I discussed yesterday, when there was a briefing on the 1st of June -- a document highlighting briefing that was to take place on the 3rd of June. I know that on the 9th of June there was a directive that the 1st Krajina Corps received and they were operating on that directive. General Talic on the same day -- on the 9th or 10th sent out his own corps-wide instruction for combat operations, which did two things: One was to secure territory; and the second was to prepare operations in the wider corridor area. He did that between the 10th of June and round about the 20th of June, 24th of June. When Operation Corridor was formally instigated, on the 24th of June, elements of the 1st Krajina Corps, the East Bosnia Corps, Milan Maric's MUP from Knin, and Veljko Milankovic and others took part in Operation Corridor from the 24th of June. They succeeded in achieving their goal of maintaining or getting a corridor link by the 4th of July, so within about ten days. They then spent a few days pushing to the Sava River, and they spent some rest of the summer expanding the corridor. But to all intents and purposes, the formal operation was announced on the 24th of June. It succeeded in obtaining the corridor by the 4th of July. The corridor was never severed in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the time of the announcement of the strategic objective to the time of the accomplishment of strategic objective number 2 was a period of about seven weeks.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, just for your -- Your Honours' information - I won't go through these documents, but I'll describe them very briefly - tabs 62 and 62.1, these are documents from various authorities congratulating other entities within the service of the 1st Krajina Corps, sending them their congratualations for successfully completing Operation Corridor. And tab 63, you will find a -- on the last page, page 6 of that document, you will find a -- a statement that is -- we have a CD. We will submit the CD. Now, General Talic, who is the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, this is a statement he makes apparently on the 30th of June, 1992, in which he says, among other things, "You know that we have achieved our aim of linking up with the East Bosnia Corps and further on with Mother Serbia." And he says that -- toward the end he says that "We must be united in realising our common goal. When I say 'united' I mean all Serbs throughout the former Yugoslavia." I won't dwell on those documents; those are contextual documents. And if we could then change -- we'll start with another topic, which was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, in your report at paragraph 2.2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if we move to the next subject -- it's twenty minutes to 6.00, I'd prefer to have a break now and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, once the witness is brought into the courtroom ... Mr. Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, whilst the witness is being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- if I could just raise a point. Your Honours will recall that during the last session, Mr. Krajisnik was having some trouble keeping up with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- the documentation. And Mr. Krajisnik asked me to ask Mr. Harmon if we could ensure that there was just an indication of an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That would make it a lot easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise, I will assist, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that my Cyrillic is very well, but usually I find the relevant pages. And I'm just looking at how much Cyrillic is about to arrive. Not much.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I must say my Cyrillic is not that impressive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Brown. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, we're going to deal very, very briefly with what is found in paragraph 2.2 of your report, which deals with the description in general terms of the nature of the 1st Krajina Corps operations generally to seize control and secure territory claimed by the Serbs. And if we could turn very briefly, Mr. Brown - because I'd like to try to complete the examination or a large part of it today - turn to tab 64. This -- in tab 64, if I could refer you to page 4 of that document. This is a 1st Krajina Corps command -- it's from the 1st Krajina Corps command and is dated the 9th of June, and it's to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- 670th, and I don't know what that -- those initials mean. Can you help me out?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's pontoon battalion, I think it was. It was an engineering unit of the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it is ERN, last three digits, 872.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in respect of that, I have given the witness a complete set of binders. Is -- usually I don't refer to the first -- I usually refer to the documents by tab numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm -- since this -- you are referring to page 4 in the English translation, which equals to last three digits 872 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Well ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we look at this document very briefly, Mr. Brown. I want to direct your attention to the thesis that you espouse in your report that the operations were designed to secure and control territory. Specifically I direct your attention to page 8, that is, 01105461 ERN. And if you see the subpart C on that page, there is a reference to a -- an order to the 30th PD to take measures to achieve full control over the territory. And if you go down to subpart 5.11, an order to the 122nd engineering unit you've described, set up measures to achieve full control over the territory. Is this a reflection of what you meant in your report when you said "efforts were designed to achieve full control over the territory," Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document I referenced earlier that has, to all intents and purposes, two components. One is to -- subordinate units to establish control over the territory, and the other, to conduct operations in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's focus on the integrated effort to achieve the strategic objectives after their announcement at the 16th Session. And I'd like to refer you to a series of documents, if I could, starting with the document found at tab 66. This, Mr. Brown, is the document which is the conclusions of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most dated the 30th of May, 1992. And in subpart A, it identifies 12 people, members of the Crisis Staff, each one having a clear domain of activities. Can you identify the members of the VRS who are in this -- VRS or -- well, actually strike that. Number 7 identifies Nedjo Anicic, and number 10 identifies Branko Basara, who's a 6th Krajina Corps commander. Can you give us your insight into this document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this would seem to be one of the examples whereby Crisis Staffs brought together military, police, TO, civilian leadership, and this is in relation to Sanski Most. Colonel Basara we've talked about before. And Nedjo Anicic was the commander of the -- the Territorial Defence in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these people are becoming members of the Crisis Staff, a political entity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would appear so from this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at the -- one of the conclusions under subpart 2, is also -- it says, and I quote, at the bottom of page 1, almost at the bottom, it says, "Also make contact with the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Krajina regarding implementation of the idea on resettlement of the population." How do you interpret that, Mr. Brown, based on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents you've seen?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would seem to indicate that there was some relationship between the Crisis Staff and the regional authority, and they're discussing the issue of resettlement, which would presumably as a result of the actions that had happened prior to this date. They also talk about "a long-term solution needs to be found from the problem of refugees from the Mahala area," which was a Muslim area. So it's clear that they were talking about the resettlement of Serb, I would say, from the area of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, tab 67. This is dated the 19th of June, 1992. It's a -- the conclusions of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff. And it identifies, does it not, Mr. Anicic, who was the TO commander, and Mr. Basara, who was the VRS commander, as being permanent members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it also references that permanent members -- above the listing of names, that permanent members of the Crisis Staff "meet every day and take decisions which everyone -- everybody else is obliged to implement."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, it would highlight this issue of cooperation -- cooperation between the military and political leadership and -- in this municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you generally comment, and then we'll look at some other documents, on the cooperation between the military and the SDS and the political authorities that you saw in the area of the ARK. So a general overview, and then we'll reference some documents.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw -- from the documentation, I was able to view significant cooperation in the ARK area. General Talic was a member of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff, which included police, SDS, and political leaders. I saw some documentation from a number of municipalities where military commanders were either, in this case, a permanent member or another is briefed or appeared to be ex officio members. I saw that in Kotor Varos, Sanski Most, Prijedor, I believe also in Kljuc, and it seemed to me that the Crisis Staff were very much an important feature of the operations in -- in -- in the Krajina in bringing together the political, military, and police bodies in order to conduct their respective works and in order to seize control of territory that they deemed to be theirs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look at some additional documents in that respect. If we could turn to tab 68. This is an extract from the minutes of a -- of a Crisis Staff meeting that took place on the 7th of July, 1992. And if you could go to item 3, and at the end of the list of people, could you comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is another example where it highlights that "Participating in the work of the War Presidency shall be Lieutenant Colonel Peulic." Colonel Peulic was the commander of the -- well, he was concurrently commander of the 122nd Brigade, which was one to have brigades that we just highlighted in that document on the 10th -- or the 9th of June. And he was also what was Operations Group Vlasic, which with was slightly larger military group under Talic, which contained a number of Brigades. So he was, in essence, the military commander that covered Kotor Varos, Skender Vakuf, and -- in that area. And he would seem to be participating -- and in fact, there are other documents, I think, from Kotor Varos which indicate that he's briefing and he's present at a number of Crisis Staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could turn to the next tab, 69.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This would appear to be a --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just wait a minute, Mr. Brown, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 69, Mr. Brown, is a document from the Celinac Municipality War Presidency dated the 23rd of July, 1992, and it is a decision on the status of the non-Serbian population of Celinac. Can you give me your observations on this document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document seems to outline a decision that severely restricts what the non-Serb population in Celinac are allowed to do. And it lists in Article 5, for example, all the issues that they're forbidden to do, including lingering on streets, bathing, using telephones --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, without giving us a description of the contents because the Judges will have an opportunity to see that, my question should have been more precise: How does this relate to coordination and cooperation with the military?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the distribution, it's sent to the Celinac -- or the commander of the Celinac Light Infantry Brigade, so I assume that they felt there was a need to disseminate this decision to them for some purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could go to another municipality now. Mr. Brown, I'm referring to tab 70. And this is a document from the Kljuc Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff War Presidency; it's a report. It is dated July of 1992, and it's a report, then, between the period of 15 May 1992 and July of 1992. And in its report at page 3 of the document, it talks about -- "Throughout the armed conflict, representatives, commanders of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina regularly participated in sessions of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency." And it goes on to say that "These representatives were in command of and conducted combat activities to defend the territory and the citizens of Kljuc municipality against Muslim extremists in good cooperation and coordination with the Crisis Staff of the Kljuc municipality. All major questions relating to the army and police were resolved within the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly. The period can be described as one of very successful cooperation between the Crisis Staff and military organs in crushing armed resistance by Muslim extremists. The Crisis Staff of the municipality paid special tribute to the 30th Division of the 1st Corps for a job well done in crushing armed resistance." Can you give us your comments on this document, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would seem to very much echo some of the other documentation from other municipalities that the military and the civilian and the police cooperated at the Crisis Staff, and it was a vehicle where they -- they operated together. The reference to the 30th Division: I know that the 1st Partizan Brigade, as it was called prior to the transition, was one of the units that was involved in operations in Kljuc in the early part of June 1992, so I'm assuming that they're passing on their congratualations to that unit. That's the same unit, by the way, that was also on that stamp for the passing of the strategic goals a couple of days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn -- turn to tab 74. This is from the -- the ARK War Staff of Banja Luka to the municipality president from Radoslav Brdjanin, who was identified as the president. Can you discuss with the Court what this document represents.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This seems to be a list of members of the Autonomous Region of Krajina War Staff and which links in political -- political members, members of the SDS, General Talic, Stojan Zupljanin, who was head of the CSB in Banja Luka, and it would seem to highlight at the regional level there was a Crisis Staff fulfilling a similar function. I would also possibly like to draw your attention to number 15, Nenad Stevandic, whom I believe is referenced in that paramilitary document. Maybe if I could check that, but I've got a feeling that he is referenced in that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is dated the 6th of May, 1992. If we could turn to tab 75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just not to make any mistakes, Stevandic was of the SOS, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, those -- those documents showed the integration into a -- a joint effort -- a coordination between military, the political authorities, as well as some police authorities. I'd like to focus your attention on the document that I've just referred to in tab 75, which is a 1 Krajina Corps report to the Main Staff of the army. It's a regular combat report. It is signed by General Talic at the end of the document. And if I can direct your attention to paragraph 2 of the document, starting with "The combat disposition of the units." Could you look at that first paragraph and give us your observations about it.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would seem to highlight that there was cooperation between the Ministry of the Interior, the police, and the military in -- they call mopping-up the terrain and confiscating weapons that, I believe, would link to the issue of weapon deadlines that were issued in a number of municipalities in the Krajina, in Prijedor, in Sanski Most, in Kljuc. And I know from other documentation -- from police documentation they also referenced that they were involved in combat operations in those municipalities and that cooperation existed there at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further to the issue of cooperation, again, in terms of the implementation of the strategic objectives and the joint operations of the authorities, if I could turn your attention to tab 76. Mr. Brown, this is a report that is prepared by the Serbian Ministry of the Interior. And it relates -- it relates what has occurred in a number of municipalities in the area of responsibility of the 1 Krajina Corps. Prijedor is mentioned; Sanski Most, on page 6; Bosanski Novi, on page 8. And in it -- and this document is a report concerning the situation as found in questions relating to prisoners, collection centres, resettlement, and the role of the police in connection with those activities. And I'd like to turn your attention, if I could, to page 2 of the document, and page 2 deals with the municipality of Prijedor. Could you look at page 2, the -- the two paragraphs at the bottom, Mr. Brown. And in respect of the coordination of police and military and the Crisis Staff and the transfer of people from that municipality to detention centres, could you give us your observations.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the document speaks for itself. It's actually also, I believe, corroborated by other military documents, too. But it would seem to me that this document is very rich, both in terms of Prijedor and the other municipalities, in highlighting this issue of police-military cooperation and in Crisis Staff and -- as well. It discusses that the army generally brought prisoners to detention centres; these detention centres were invariably organised or run by the police. And then the document also, I believe, discusses the numbers of people who have left either prior to the combat operations or who are in detention centres or who are leaving, they say, voluntarily, either registering or unregistering their property. And I think it's a very large document, but it's quite rich, and I think it -- it highlights very well this issue of cooperation, both in terms of moving people into detention centres and those camps that were -- that were established and what was happening to the population in those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say at -- can you give us -- this is a very dense document, Mr. Brown, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is a document I think we could spend a lot of time discussing. Unfortunately, that is something I don't have, but I'd like to take you to some highlights in this, if I can. I'd invite your brief comments, Mr. Brown. There is a reference to the army transporting people and joint teams of police and military interrogating those people in this document, is there not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find that to be a common feature of the documentation that you reviewed, that there would be a -- a coordinated effort by the army and the police to capture, detain, incarcerate, and interrogate non- Serbs; those were joint operations?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this document highlights -- does seem to highlight that, and there are other documents that show a relationship -- for example, in this document, page 3, they discuss the categorisation of prisoners. I know of another documentation in Sanski Most that discusses the issue of categorisation, which would seem to include both the military and the police involved in that process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that -- that generally this report especially highlights that individuals were taken by the army. I think in Novi it was members of the TO as well as the JNA. But it tends to be that the army was taking people to these detention centres and that the police were invariably running them. And then there is also this cooperation in some cases highlighted whereby prisoners were moved from these detention camps to Manjaca army camp, which was run by the 1st Krajina Corps. So that in itself, both in some military documentation as well as this documentation, or the three municipal reports which this report forms the basis of, highlights the joint nature of -- of that process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it also identifies the number of people in detention facilities at various times, does it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does in some detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I'm not going to spend more time on this particular document, but I would like to inform you that there are other documents that are inserted in this binder that relate to this document. From what I see from this document, each of these municipalities prepared a report that was sent to a commission. I've included each of the individual municipality reports that were sent that form the basis of this document. In respect of Bosanski Novi, you'll find that - I don't ask you to look at it - but you'll find that at tab 50. In respect of the Prijedor report that was sent to the commission, you'll find that at tab 77.1. So in -- and in response to the Sanski Most report that formed the basis of this document, you'll find that at tab 77. That's just for your own guidance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for me, Mr. Harmon, I -- after 76, there seems to be no 77, but we were just provided with a 77.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was informed of that just now, Your Honour, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- some reconstruction of this document -- of this binder that needs to be done, so ... But you will see in the tabs that I had mentioned, Your Honour, that these are documents that gave rise to the final report that I was referred to with Mr. Brown a few minutes ago. Now, Your Honour, if you need more time to examine your binders, if you'd let me know. Otherwise, I could proceed to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will consult the portions you just mentioned being at the basis of that report. So the binder now jumps from 76 to 77.1. It -- and then to 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour should have -- I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm the only one -- I should not talk on behalf of the Chamber, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm the only one who's doing without, but I'll borrow one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have -- we have one for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can proceed? Yes. Thank you. If we could turn to the document at tab 78. This is, Your Honours, a slightly extended report from Prijedor. It covers a greater period of time. The report from the commission was in August. This covers the last nine months of the work of the public security section in Prijedor. It's dated January 1993, and it's from the Minister of the Interior in Banja Luka. It's an extensive report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Brown, I'd like you to comment on its contents in respect of the cooperation between the army and the police in military operations, and I direct your attention to page 4 of the document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would seem to echo a little bit of what -- what was articulated in the previous Prijedor report or the Prijedor section. It also reflects that combat report that indicated that the police were assisting in combat operations in Prijedor. And this section, paragraph 4, outlines that the police were involved in combat operations in the particular villages in -- in Prijedor, Kozarac, Kozorusa, Trnopolje and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I do not see any paragraph on page 4, and for Mr. Krajisnik's information it seems to be page 3 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 4 under paragraph B, participation of the members of the station in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, could you also turn to the next page. It actually quantifies, does it not, the number of hours that the police in Prijedor served in combat operations, does it not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the above paragraph also highlights the other municipalities that they were -- they were engaged in, so it wasn't exclusively just Prijedor. And then the section below the table in the middle of the page talks about the establishment of Keraterm, Trnopolje, Omarska, and the number of interviews that they conducted in those camps. And it states here that "Except for Trnopolje, the reception centres were dismantled on the 21st of August, 1992."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you: In respect of these camps, at the end it talks about -- at the end of page 5, it talks about persons who had spent time in Omarska and Keraterm, and then it says, "Several convoys were organised for -- for the transportation of these persons to Skender Vakuf, Bugojno." Was that territory that was outside the territory controlled and occupied by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skender Vakuf and Bugojno actually sat on the -- the border between the RS territory and Central Bosnia, and I believe that's where bus convoys would travel to, that border area in Skender Vakuf and Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And deposit people who were to be transported out of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, that was on page 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me go back to page 4 with an ERN number of 01108987, subpart B. And this indicates that there were combat operations conducted by the police in part with others in the various locations, most intensively in Kozarac, Hambarine, in Prijedor itself, and that "the police were engaged in intensive mopping-up activities in those locations." Do you know what happened in those locations to the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were moved out -- or many of those villages were moved out to Omarska, Trnopolje, or Keraterm camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it on the basis of documents that you have this knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go, if we can, Mr. Brown, to the subject of disarming, and if I can direct your attention to the first document on that subject. And you mentioned, Mr. Brown, you mentioned in your expert report that disarming of the non-Serb population was part of a pattern that you saw in the military documentation. You discuss that pattern on page 61 of your report at paragraph 2.4. And you say, Mr. Brown, in that report that the pattern that you observed based on the documentation would include "the movement of forces into the areas of non-Serb areas prior to combat activity, an overwhelming military response to low-level" -- "relatively low-level events, the issuance of deadlines for the handing-over of weapons and/or personnel, the shelling, attacking, and destruction of villages and towns, cooperation with the TO and police units, the forcible movement in sections of the population for questioning and detention at interrogation centres and camps, looting, killings, and the movement out of many of the non-Serbs from the area." Now, Mr. Brown, let's -- I'd like to focus on at least one -- we're going to focus on all of the elements that you've just described as part of the pattern that you saw in the documentation. If we could turn to tab 71, and the document that you have before you is a Kljuc Municipality Crisis Staff order that was issued on the 28th of May, 1992, at 8.00 in the morning. And could you look at subpart 1 and explain subpart 1 of this order that was issued by the president of the Crisis Staff, Jovo Banjac.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This references or calls for "All citizens who own illegally acquired weapons to hand them over and a particular deadline on that day; otherwise, vigorous measures would be implemented to carry out disarmament." And I have seen in a number of municipalities this very same issue of deadlines being -- being given. I saw it in Bosanski Novi, in Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, Celinac, I believe. And as I've mentioned earlier on, I noted that there appeared to be a relationship between the instruction that came out in April, the Subotic instruction, an ARK decision that came out in early May, and various Crisis Staff decisions that came in municipal -- municipal Crisis Staffs relating to this issue of disarmament, invariably with a deadline. And most often the deadline on expiring would result in combat operations. So I think the issue of deadlines and potentially very important, and it did seem to occur in a number of municipalities in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of non-compliance with deadlines, what happened? What happened to the non- -- the civilian population, the non-Serb civilian population as a result of non-compliance with the deadlines, from what you can see in the documentation, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the documentation I can see, after the deadlines expired, areas were attacked by Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of the non-Serbs were rounded up, sent for questioning, and a significant number appeared in the detention camps that are highlighted by these police documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we turn to the document at tab 79, which also is a document that references -- strike that. This references Kljuc, but this is a document that is dated the 28th of May, 1992, and it's a regular combat report from the Sipovo command post to the command of the 30th Infantry Division. And if I could draw your attention, Mr. Brown, to page 2, the second paragraph above the bottom line. And this is ERN number 03009308. Could you direct your attention to that paragraph, please, Mr. Brown, and explain what --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the paragraph that starts "Because of the situation ..."?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct, "Because of the situation in Kljuc."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The 3rd Battalion of the first infantry brigade was made fully combat ready as ordered. If the Muslims do not surrender their weapons by 27 May 1992 at 1200 hours, the battalion will carry out a mopping-up operation." This is the battalion that fell under the 30th Division that was congratulated in the previous document from the Kljuc Crisis Staff report, and I know that this battalion, the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Infantry Brigade, was involved in combat operations in Kljuc in the days following this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This use of the term "mopping-up," what -- can you tell the Court what that term means in military terms and what it meant in -- to you in reviewing these documents.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what "mopping-up" means from my perspective as an ex-army officer, which normally means small, already broken up, fragmented units that might have to be cleared up in an area that you've already generally conducted operations in. Well, I'm not sure that they use that phrase with that meaning here because the result of this operation in Kljuc was that areas were attacked and people were brought to detention centres, and it's -- it's not a phrase that -- or the operation appeared to be carried out in Kljuc is not one that I would classify as a -- as a mopping-up operation, from my military experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This unit that's going to be doing the mopping-up is mentioned on page 1 in the table on the right-hand side as comprising 269 people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It wasn't the only unit that was involved in Kljuc. Actually, there were -- there were other -- other units, as well, but this was one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to look at two -- two orders, if we could, that relate to Sanski Most and relate to this topic that we're talking about. The first is found in tab 80, and this is from the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most, and it's dated the 23rd of May, 1992. And in sub- -- it's a conclusion of the Crisis Staff, and in subpart 3 it says, "The question of disarming paramilitary formations of armed individuals implement the conclusions of the previous Crisis Staff meeting, issue a proclamation to the radio station on Saturday, 23 May 1992 to be read out every 20 minutes." Now, that's on the 23rd of May. And if we could turn to tab -- the document in tab 81, also from Sanski Most. This is a document issued by the Territorial Defence commander, Colonel Anicic, who we have earlier seen, I believe, as a member of the Crisis Staff. And this is an order for a disarmament operation. What is this document, Mr. Brown? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order to -- to the Territorial Defence to -- along with, in fact, the 6th Brigade to conduct operations in the, I believe, Mahala area and other non-Serb areas, Mahala, Otoka, in order, to they say, disarm -- disarm those settlements. And it makes reference to the 6th Brigade as being engaged in that, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Down in paragraph 2, the references in paragraph 2, three lines from the bottom -- or four lines from the bottom, it says, "Maintain in coordinated action with units of the 6th Brigade complete control of the territory in order to ensure stable functioning of our government and to create conditions for unobstructed life and work."
